1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3.strategy: Retakes with a developing move. White has now moved both centre pawns, so both bishops are free, and the pawn bought quick pieces and play on the open c- and d-files; Black is a pawn up but has no piece out and two bishops locked behind pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nf3.strategy: Offers a second pawn: after ...cxb2 the recapture Bxb2 gives White a bishop on the long diagonal and quick development, but only for two pawns. That is too much to give for the compensation; Black simply takes and keeps a clear material edge.
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nf3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Danish Variation

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6.strategy: The most flexible reply: it develops a piece and controls d4 and e5, so White cannot push the e-pawn yet, and Black can later develop the king's bishop without Qd4 hitting b4 and g7. Black starts the task of untangling against White's lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 d6.strategy: Controls e5 so White cannot gain space there, and opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop. It builds a compact pawn wall, but it commits the d-pawn before any piece is out, so Black still has all of its development to do against White's lead.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and covers d5, a solid reply that also softens the bishop's pressure on f7 in advance. The king stays in the centre, though, and a knight sacrifice on d5 that opens the e-file is always a tactical idea for White.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 g6.strategy: Heads for a fianchetto, where the bishop on g7 pressures the knight on c3 along the long diagonal. Sound but slow: a flank pawn move while White is already developing, and if ...e6 follows as well the dark squares around the king become weak.
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defence
